_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Wild Spaces & Outdoor Life' through a RURAL TECH AND INNOVATION lens. Strong fits include: wildfire detection tech and BC Wildfire monitoring systems, satellite/drone surveillance for Chilcotin wilderness, wildlife tracking and conservation technology, watershed sensors and salmon habitat monitoring, weather stations and climate tracking in backcountry, avalanche forecasting tech, trail mapping and GPS systems, outdoor recreation apps and connectivity, backcountry communication devices (satellite messengers, Meshtastic), flood/drought prediction systems, remote cameras for wildlife research, and how technology helps manage and protect Cariboo wild spaces. Prefer articles that bridge wilderness/conservation AND technology. Penalise heavily (score 0–20): prehistoric and ancient biology (fossils, palaeontology, deep-time creatures) with no contemporary conservation technology angle — these belong to Sunday's Science theme; AI and data centre infrastructure stories about business strategy, investment, or corporate politics rather than direct wilderness, ecosystem, or land-use impact in BC; geopolitical conflict, war, and crime news with no outdoor or conservation relevance; consumer tech reviews and financial market stories; general political and judicial news. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

Amid the avalanche of policy announcements, platform promises and attack ads, it can be hard to know where party leaders really stand on the issues. Mario Canseco of Research Co. regularly polls British Columbian voters to ask which issues they care most about. For the past three years, housing has led. This year, it is cost-of-living. In a poll conducted on Oct. 13, the economy/jobs was the top issue for 25 per cent of respondents; housing/poverty/homelessness for 23 per cent; healthcare for 21 per cent, and crime/public safety for nine per cent. With the cost of living the top issue for most voters, economic concerns moved to the forefront as the campaigns hit the home stretch. A back-and-forth emerged as campaigns questioned each other’s math and whether spending or tax-cut promises are realistic. After 10 years in power, the NDP is defending its economic record amid historic deficits. The party’s main new plank is a proposed income tax hike on the wealthiest 3.88 per cent of British Columbians. The NDP says it would spend the extra money on new health-care facilities, child care centres and schools, slowly lowering the deficit over the next three years. The B.C. Conservative Party promises to cut taxes by raising the personal income tax exemption. This would essentially give everyone a $1,000 break. The party also promises new spending and a reduced deficit. Much of this relies on extremely optimistic economic growth, far beyond what banks and academic experts forecast. The B.C. items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive

The cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze.

In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves.
